Battle of Ba-tosh. In the spring of 1885, a Canadian army marched north across the prairies to the May-tee village of Ba-tosh. For four days a few hundred men in rifle pits held it off. On the fourth day, the army broke through. These events were long called the North-West Rebellion. Today they are more often called the North-West Resistance, the name used by Parks Canada and the May-tee Nation.

The May-tee of the South Saskatchewan. The May-tee are a people born of the fur trade, with First Nations and European roots, their own language, Mitchif, and their own way of life on the plains: buffalo hunting, freighting and farming. Many had moved west from Red River, in Manitoba, after 1870. At Ba-tosh and the nearby settlements they farmed long, narrow river lots running back from the South Saskatchewan, as they had at Red River. The village took its name from its founder, the trader Zav-yay Luh-tondr, known as Ba-tosh. It had a ferry on the Carlton Trail, stores, houses and a new church, San-tan-twan duh Pa-doo.

Grievances. By the 1880s the buffalo were gone. The Cree and other First Nations who had signed treaties faced hunger, and felt that the government was not keeping its promises. The May-tee feared for their land. Government surveyors used square lots, and title to the river lots was slow to come. Year after year they sent petitions to Ottawa, with little answer. In 1884 a group of May-tee, Gabriel Doo-mon among them, rode to Montana to ask Louis Ree-el to come back and lead them. Ree-el had led the Red River Resistance of 1869 and 1870, which brought Manitoba into Canada, and had lived in exile since.

March 1885. In March 1885 Ree-el and his followers declared a provisional government at Ba-tosh. Gabriel Doo-mon, a buffalo hunter famous on the plains, led its fighters. On the 26th of March, at Duck Lake, May-tee and First Nations fighters defeated a force of North-West Mounted Police and volunteers. Further west, Cree warriors took Frog Lake and Fort Pitt. Ottawa sent an army west on the new Canadian Pacific Railway, still unfinished in places north of Lake Superior. Its commander was a British officer, Major-General Frederick Middleton.

The road to Ba-tosh. Middleton marched north from the railway at Ka-pell toward Ba-tosh. On the 24th of April, at Fish Creek, Doo-mon's men ambushed his column from a wooded koo-lee and stopped it. That battle has its own page. Middleton waited about two weeks for supplies, more men, and a river steamer, the Northcote. Then, on the 7th of May, he marched on Ba-tosh.

The armies and the ground. Middleton counted 886 men on land: militia from Winnipeg, Toronto and Ontario towns, mounted scouts, and gunners of A Battery. He had four nine-pounder guns, a Gatling gun, and about fifty more men on the steamer. The defenders were May-tee, with Cree and Dakota allies: perhaps 250 to 300 at the start. They had hunting rifles, shotguns and old muzzle-loaders, and little ammunition. The village lay on the east bank of the river. To the south, the church and the rectory stood on higher ground, with the cemetery beyond. Along the wooded slopes and ravines, the defenders had dug rifle pits: shallow holes with a low wall of earth and logs, hard to see and hard to hit.
Middleton plans a joint attack. His column will come up from the south-east by land, while the Northcote, with soldiers behind barricades on her decks, comes down the river behind the village.

The Northcote arrives before the land column is ready. Fighters on both banks open fire on her. At the Ba-tosh ferry, the ferryman Alex Fisher, helped by Pass-kal Mon-toor, has lowered the ferry cable across the river. It catches the steamer and knocks down her smokestacks. Damaged, she drifts on downstream and never lands her soldiers.

The column reaches the church and the rectory. The priests, the sisters, and May-tee women and children are sheltering inside. A bullet through the rectory wall wounds Father Moo-lan in the leg. A white cloth is shown, and Middleton orders the firing stopped.

Beyond the church, the ground drops toward the river. The soldiers push to the edge of Mission Ridge and run into fire from pits they cannot see. The guns are pulled forward onto the ridge, and the defenders creep through the bush toward them. Captain Howard's Gatling gun opens fire and covers the infantry as they fall back.

When the Northcote came by, Philippe Gar-no took about twenty men from the pits to fire on her. That thinned the line facing Middleton's first advance. The defenders, scouts under Patrice Flur-ee and Om-bwahz Shom-pan-yuh watching both banks, also pressed the soldiers' flanks. Hildebrandt argues that these May-tee attacks deserve more credit than the usual story gives them.
Middleton pulls his army back into a camp walled with wagons and earth, a za-ree-ba, about a kilometre south-east of the church. Through the night, rifle fire from the bush keeps the camp awake.

The soldiers move out again, cautiously. They dig shallow pits halfway toward the cemetery but cannot take the heights. The guns shell the rifle pits, the cemetery and the buildings across the river. The camp's walls are built higher.

Middleton rides out with mounted men onto the open prairie to the north-east and fires a few shells. Defenders hurry across to meet him, and he sees that the line in front of his infantry grows thin when they do.

In the pits, cartridges are running out. Witnesses describe men searching the ground the soldiers have left for dropped cartridges, and melting down lead. Later stories say they fired nails and stones; that has not been proven.
Middleton tries the trick again. He leads the mounted men and a gun out onto the Zho-lee Prairie, to draw the defenders north. The infantry are to attack when they hear his guns.
The infantry do not move. Perhaps the wind carried the sound away, or the order was not clear. Middleton rides back angry, and his men go to lunch.

In the afternoon the Midland and the Grenadiers, with the 90th Winnipeg Rifles beside them, go forward near the cemetery, and the advance becomes a rush. Who ordered it is still argued: Lieutenant-Colonel Williams, Colonel Van Straw-ben-zee, or nobody, as the soldiers simply ran forward. The thin line in the pits breaks.

The soldiers pour down toward the village. Fighting goes on in the bush and around the houses. Captain John French of French's Scouts is shot at an upstairs window of Ba-tosh's house. Prisoners held by the May-tee are set free. Among the defenders killed that day is Joseph Wel-ett, an old man, said to be over ninety.
Ba-tosh has fallen. Families who had sheltered by the river come out to find their homes searched and their belongings taken. Some later testified that soldiers took a woman's wedding ring.

The army won. Hildebrandt counts 25 dead in the four days, on both sides. By the last day, only 50 to 60 defenders were still fighting, with about 40 rifles between them. On the 15th of May, Louis Ree-el gave himself up. Gabriel Doo-mon stayed near Ba-tosh for some days; when he heard that Ree-el had surrendered, he escaped to the United States. That summer, the Cree chiefs Poundmaker and Big Bear also surrendered, and were sent to prison. Ree-el was tried for high treason at Regina. The jury found him guilty but asked for mercy. He was hanged on the 16th of November 1885. Eleven days later, eight Cree and Assiniboine men were hanged together at Battleford. Ree-el's death divided Canada for a generation, French against English, Catholic against Protestant. Doo-mon later toured the United States with Buffalo Bill's Wild West show. After an amnesty he came home, and he died near Ba-tosh in 1906. Today Ba-tosh is a National Historic Site. Ree-el, once hanged as a traitor, is remembered as the founder of Manitoba, and statues of Ree-el and Doo-mon stand in Winnipeg and Saskatoon.

The village took its name from its founder, the trader Zav-yay Luh-tondr, known as Ba-tosh. It had a ferry on the Carlton Trail, stores, houses and a new church, San-tan-twan duh Pa-doo.

He had four nine-pounder guns, a Gatling gun, and about fifty more men on the steamer. The defenders were May-tee, with Cree and Dakota allies: perhaps 250 to 300 at the start. Beyond the church, the ground drops toward the river. The soldiers push to the edge of Mission Ridge and run into fire from pits they cannot see. The guns are pulled forward onto the ridge, and the defenders creep through the bush toward them. Captain Howard's Gatling gun opens fire and covers the infantry as they fall back.

Middleton pulls his army back into a camp walled with wagons and earth, a za-ree-ba, about a kilometre south-east of the church. Through the night, rifle fire from the bush keeps the camp awake.

Middleton rides out with mounted men onto the open prairie to the north-east and fires a few shells. Defenders hurry across to meet him, and he sees that the line in front of his infantry grows thin when they do.
